body.hook: Why does your eye go straight to the one red umbrella in a crowd of grey ones? Designers control where you look using principles of design. Learn them and you can steer any viewer's eye.

study.title: Steer the Eye
study.question: How do the principles of design control where we look?
study.passage:
Studio steps (written for this lesson):
1. Principle hunt (15 minutes): Look at four artworks or posters (for example, a Henri Matisse cut-out such as The Snail, 1953; a movie poster; a Bridget Riley op-art painting; a photo of a single red umbrella in a grey crowd). For each, find the focal point and name the principles that create it.
2. Mini-studies (25 minutes): Divide a page into four boxes. In each, use simple cut paper shapes to show one principle: emphasis (one shape different in colour or size), rhythm (repeated shapes with spacing that changes), unity (similar colours and shapes that belong together) and contrast (black and white, big and small).
3. Gallery walk: Classmates guess which principle each box shows.
study.source: Original activity written for this lesson; teachers show images from public museum websites.

body.objective: Students will be able to create a relief print.
body.iCan: I can create a relief print.
successCriteria: I can design an image that works as a print
I can carve a relief block safely

body.hook: Before printing presses, every copy of a picture had to be drawn by hand. Relief printing changed that: carve a block once, ink it, and print it a hundred times. Albrecht Dürer, Japanese ukiyo-e artists and Inuit printmakers in Kinngait (Cape Dorset) all used versions of it.

vocabulary.definition: A print made by carving away parts of a block so the raised areas print.
A surface such as linoleum or foam that is carved for printing.
A small roller used to spread ink.
A print appears backwards compared with the block.
A set of matching prints from the same block.
Lining up the paper and block so each print is in the same place.

study.title: Make Your Mark
study.question: How does relief printing let artists make multiple images?
study.passage:
Studio steps (written for this lesson):
1. Look: Study prints from Kinngait Studios in Nunavut (founded 1959), such as works by Kenojuak Ashevak, and Hokusai's woodblock prints. Notice bold shapes and strong contrast between inked and uninked areas.
2. Design (15 minutes): Draw a 10 cm × 15 cm design using bold shapes, emphasis and pattern. Remember that any text must be backwards on the block. Shade the parts that will print (stay raised).
3. Transfer and carve (two lessons for lino, one for foam): Transfer the design to the block. With lino cutters, always cut away from your body with your other hand behind the cutter, using a bench hook. Carve away the white areas.
4. Print: Roll ink thinly with the brayer until it looks like velvet. Ink the block, place paper, rub with a baren or spoon, and peel.
5. Edition: Make three matching prints. Sign each in pencil below the image: title, edition number (1/3, 2/3, 3/3) and your name.
study.source: Original activity written for this lesson; teachers show images of Kinngait and ukiyo-e prints from public sources.

body.objective: Students will be able to construct a 3-D form.
successCriteria: I can construct a 3-D form from card or paper
I can use joining techniques so my form stands
I can apply design principles in three dimensions
body.hook: Walk around a sculpture and it changes with every step. Unlike a drawing, a 3-D form has to work from every side, stand up by itself and hold together. Today you build in three dimensions.

vocabulary.definition: A shape with height, width and depth.
A sculpture meant to be seen from all sides.
A sculpture that projects from a flat background.
A small flap used to join paper or card pieces.
An inner framework that supports a sculpture.

study.title: Build in 3-D
study.question: How do artists design forms that work from every side?
study.passage:
Studio steps (written for this lesson):
1. Look: Study 3-D works such as Louise Bourgeois's giant spider sculpture Maman (1999), which stands outside the National Gallery of Canada in Ottawa, and examples of paper engineering or origami architecture. Walk around a classroom object and sketch it from four sides.
2. Paper techniques (15 minutes): Practise scoring and folding, curling, slotting, tabbing and pleating to make shapes stand.
3. Design (10 minutes): Plan an abstract sculpture about 20 cm tall using at least three techniques and two design principles (for example rhythm through repeated curls and emphasis through one large form).
4. Build (two lessons): Construct the form in card. Use tabs or slots rather than lots of tape. Turn it often to check every side.
5. Display and critique: View all sculptures from four sides.
study.source: Original activity written for this lesson; teachers show images of Maman from public sources.
